name: thresh
summary: Each side guards a hearth that never moves; take the other hearth to win.
A scythe runs up to three cells along a line and cuts down every piece it passes, your own included.
Nothing cuts through a stone: a stone in the way stops a scythe.
A hare steps one cell, or vaults a piece next to it and lands just beyond, taking whatever stands there.
Stones step one cell in any direction and never take anything; only hares can take them.
Stones round your hearth keep the scythes out, but each one is a step an enemy hare can vault onto it.
If you cannot move, you lose.
description: A siege on a hexagonal board between two attackers that want opposite boards. The scythe wants open lines: it mows down everything it passes, hares, scythes and the hearth itself, and only a stone stops it. The hare wants a crowd: it can only take by vaulting a neighbouring piece, so on an empty board it is harmless and beside a wall it is deadly. Each hearth starts ringed by its own stones, which make it safe from scythes and give an enemy hare a way in over each of them, from the cell two steps out along the line through that stone. So the decision that keeps coming back is whether a stone is a wall or a ladder: pull it out of the ring and a scythe line opens, leave it and you must keep enemy hares off the cells beyond it. A scythe swing is never free either, since it clears your own hares from its path as readily as the enemy's, and a stone of yours walked up beside the enemy hearth is a screen they cannot cut away, because no scythe can touch it. Games open with stones and hares pushing into the middle, turn on a hare fight over the cells two steps from a hearth, and usually end when a broken ring lets a scythe through or a hare finds its vault.
